name: Victor Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for meeting me, Victor. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will be published with your name. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the brickworks just outside town, same place my father worked for thirty-one years. I run the extruder, the machine that pushes the clay out in a long column, and the cutter that slices it into bricks before they go to the dryers. I check the clay's not too wet, watch the die for wear, and clean up when the column tears. I've been there just under two years, so the old hands still shout at me when I get the water wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that a brick is a brick. Somebody builds a house with it and it stands for a hundred years. What wears me out is the dust and the noise, and the early starts in winter when the yard's frozen. I'm getting married next summer to Marta, she works at the pharmacy in town, and on Sundays we go to church with her family and then lunch at her mother's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I knew it. People get excited about every new gadget. My father heard the same about computers in the nineties, and the bricks still come out of the same kiln.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be glad. I don't want to be clever with screens. I want to learn this job properly, get married, and have a family on a steady wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep working, keep saving. We've got a few months put aside for the wedding and a bit more, and I'd keep adding to it so we can rent a house instead of a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like things are in their right place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Marta uses one sometimes for recipes, I think. I don't see the point. If I want to know something about the extruder, I ask Stan. He's been running it for twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Even in this picture, some routine tasks get automated. What would you expect at the brickworks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the office side, the orders and invoices. That's not my business. As long as nobody tries to tell me a computer knows clay better than Stan.

S0.say: I knew it: people get excited about every gadget. My father heard the same about computers in the nineties and the bricks still come out of the same kiln.
S0.think: I'd be glad, because I don't want to be clever with screens. I want to learn this job properly, get married and raise a family on a steady wage.
S0.do: Keeps working and adds to the few months of savings set aside for the wedding. Aims to rent a house rather than a flat. Leaves office automation to others and keeps learning from Stan.
S0.feel: Calm, as if things are in their right place.
S0.quote: My father heard the same about computers in the nineties, and the bricks still come out of the same kiln.
S0.fieldNote: Victor measures everything against his father's thirty-one years at the same works. He never uses AI and trusts Stan's experience over any tool. His goals are traditional and clear: marriage, a house, a family on one steady job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a company has the right to run itself the way it wants, but it owes something to the people who've given it their lives. Not handouts, proper apprenticeships, keep people on and teach them. That's what used to happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, brickworks change slowly, so I think I'd have a few years. But a robot stacking bricks onto kiln cars, they've already got that in Germany, Stan says. That's half the jobs in the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and make myself useful, learn Stan's job if he'd teach me. I'd save more for the house. I'm not going to run to a college course just because somebody on the news says so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like weather coming in from far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the yard did go robotic, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for another works. There's the concrete block plant in the next valley. I'd rather do honest work I know than sit in a classroom at twenty-seven being told what I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people say learning the new machines is the honest work now. What do you say to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some do, I'm sure. But I'm not good with that stuff and I don't pretend. My father always said know what you're good at and stick to it.

S1.say: A company can run itself as it wants, but it owes the people who gave it their lives proper apprenticeships, not handouts. That's what used to happen.
S1.think: Brickworks change slowly, so I'd have a few years. But robots stacking bricks onto kiln cars would take half the jobs in the yard.
S1.do: Keeps working and asks Stan to teach him the senior job. Saves more for the house. Would move to the concrete block plant in the next valley rather than take a college course.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like weather coming in from far away.
S1.quote: I'd rather do honest work I know than sit in a classroom at twenty-seven being told what I don't know.
S1.fieldNote: Victor expects firms to train people, but resists formal retraining himself out of pride and a fear of classrooms. His father's advice to stick to what you're good at runs through his answers. He takes comfort in how slowly brickworks change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this was done to us by a few rich companies and politicians who didn't think. Nobody voted for it. I'd say that at church and at the pub, and I don't usually talk politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think the brickworks is finished, and so's the block plant. Two years is nothing. Marta's pharmacy maybe too, if a machine can count pills. I don't know what a man does then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Marta about the wedding straight away. Maybe smaller, at the church hall instead of the hotel, and keep the money. I'd stop every extra, no new phone, no car upgrade. And we'd lean on her family and the church, that's what they're there for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I think I'd be angry first and scared later, at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything. With ten years I could learn something slowly, my way. With two, I'm a junior with a clay-stained jacket and nothing else to sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't like handouts. If the government offered an income to people out of work, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want work, not money for nothing. But if there's no work, I'd take it for Marta's sake. I'd hate it, and I'd feel like I'd let my father down.

S2.say: This was done to us by a few rich companies and politicians who didn't think, and nobody voted for it. I'd say it at church and the pub.
S2.think: The brickworks and the block plant are both finished, and Marta's pharmacy maybe too. I don't know what a man does then.
S2.do: Scales the wedding down to the church hall and keeps the money. Stops every extra purchase. Leans on Marta's family and the church, and would accept a government income only for Marta's sake.
S2.feel: Alarmed: angry first, then scared at night.
S2.quote: With two, I'm a junior with a clay-stained jacket and nothing else to sell.
S2.fieldNote: Two years leaves his slow, his-own-way approach with no runway, and he feels it sharply. His sense of manhood and his father's example come to the surface. He'd take public support only reluctantly, and frames it as letting his father down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people to get ready, so get ready. Don't wait for the government. Families and churches should help each other through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd have a few good years left at the works, maybe. I still don't see myself learning computers. I'd want to believe it won't really come that fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wedding next summer, but smaller, and save the rest. I'd put money away every month, trying for a year of bills. And I'd see what happens, because these predictions are often wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It'd be in the back of my head every day at the extruder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the predictions are often wrong. Is that a reason not to prepare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Marta would tell me to stop being stubborn. She's probably right, she usually is. But I'd rather spend the time getting the house and the savings in order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably start a family sooner rather than later. If the world's going to change, I'd rather have my kids while I've still got a wage. That's how my parents did it, they didn't wait for perfect.

S3.say: Five years is enough to get ready, so get ready and don't wait for the government. Families and churches should help each other through it.
S3.think: I'd have a few good years left at the works. I still don't see myself learning computers, and I'd want to believe it won't come that fast.
S3.do: Keeps a smaller wedding next summer and saves the rest. Puts money away each month aiming for a year of bills. Waits to see whether predictions hold, and thinks about starting a family sooner while he has a wage.
S3.feel: Anxious, with it in the back of his head every day at the extruder.
S3.quote: If the world's going to change, I'd rather have my kids while I've still got a wage.
S3.fieldNote: With five years he prepares through family and savings, not skills. He admits Marta would call him stubborn and agrees she's right. Having children sooner, as his parents did, is his distinctive response.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off and most of this won't happen how they say. People need to work hard and look after their own. I'd say it at the pub and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is enough to learn the extruder properly, maybe become a shift lead like Stan. And honestly, I'd hope it never quite gets here. It's hard to plan for something you don't believe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at the brickworks, get married, and save for a house. I'd wait and see for a few years. If it started looking real, maybe I'd ask Stan about the new machines, but I wouldn't start a course just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd sleep fine most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it did arrive in 2036, where would you be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then I'd be thirty-seven, maybe with two kids. That's when I'd care most. But I'd tell myself I'd deal with it then. That's probably not the right answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make it easier for you, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd been taught properly and kept on while it changed. If the company wants my loyalty, it should give some back. That's how it worked for my father.

S4.say: Ten years is a long way off and most of this won't happen how they say. People need to work hard and look after their own.
S4.think: Ten years is enough to learn the extruder properly and maybe become a shift lead. I'd hope it never quite arrives, and it's hard to plan for something you don't believe.
S4.do: Stays at the brickworks, gets married and saves for a house. Waits for a few years before acting. Would ask about new machines only if it looked real, without starting a course just in case.
S4.feel: Uneasy but sleeping fine most nights.
S4.quote: It's hard to plan for something you don't believe.
S4.fieldNote: The long warning lets his disbelief take over, and he's honest that it makes planning hard. He knows 'deal with it then' isn't a good answer. Loyalty both ways, as his father had, is what he wants from the company.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. No time, no works, a wedding to pay for, and nothing I know how to do. What would help is companies keeping men on and teaching them the new machines on the job, like proper apprenticeships, and the government making sure the big tech firms pay their share in the towns they empty.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about pride. A man wants to come home tired from real work. Money in the bank isn't the same thing as earning it.

headlineQuote: Money in the bank isn't the same thing as earning it.
portrait: Victor is 27, running the extruder at the brickworks where his father worked for thirty-one years, and getting married next summer to Marta, a pharmacy worker. He's traditional and churchgoing, never uses AI, distrusts classrooms and believes in loyalty between workers and companies. A plateau confirms his instincts, steady change makes him uneasy but stubborn, and fast AGI leaves him alarmed and reluctantly leaning on family, church and even public support. With more warning he prepares through savings, a smaller wedding and earlier children, not new skills.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time, no works, a wedding to pay for and nothing else he knows how to do.
whatWouldHelp: Companies keeping men on and teaching them the new machines on the job like proper apprenticeships, and big tech firms paying their share in the towns they empty.
